title: Best personal loans in Nigeria (2026)
intro: Personal loans in Nigeria range from instant app-based credit of a few thousand naira to multi-million-naira salary loans repaid over three years. The right choice depends on how fast you need the money, whether you bank where you're borrowing, and — above all — the true cost once management fees and monthly interest are added in. Headline 'monthly interest' figures can look small but compound into very high annual rates, so we convert every product to a comparable basis and show the fees alongside the rate. We list only products from institutions licensed by the Central Bank of Nigeria, and we mark which providers have been licence-checked and have claimed their listing. Use the filters to sort by interest rate, fees or loan amount, and always confirm the exact terms with the provider before you apply — the figures here are indicative and change frequently.

faq.question: How were these personal loans ranked?
faq.answer: By default we sort by customer rating, with sponsored placements clearly labelled and shown first. You can re-sort by lowest interest, lowest fees or smallest minimum amount. Ranking never affects whether a provider is shown as licence-verified — that is a separate, factual check against the CBN register.

faq.question: What does the gold Verified badge mean?
faq.answer: It means the provider has been matched to the Central Bank of Nigeria's register of licensed institutions AND has claimed and confirmed its listing with us. Unlicensed or unclaimed lenders never receive the gold badge, even if they are popular.

faq.question: Are these interest rates and fees guaranteed?
faq.answer: No. All rates, fees and terms shown are indicative only and can change at any time. Each product shows the date we last verified its figures. Always confirm the exact terms directly with the provider before applying.

faq.question: What do I usually need to apply for a personal loan in Nigeria?
faq.answer: Most lenders require your Bank Verification Number (BVN) and a valid ID. Salary loans typically also need recent bank statements and proof of employment. Each product page lists the specific required documents.

faq.question: How can I reduce the cost of a personal loan?
faq.answer: Compare the all-in cost, not just the headline rate: a loan with a low monthly interest but a high management fee can cost more than one with a slightly higher rate and no fee. Shorter tenures usually mean less total interest. Use our loan repayment calculator to estimate the total you'll repay.

faq.question: Is a fixed deposit better than a regular savings account?
faq.answer: Fixed deposits usually pay a higher, guaranteed rate but lock your money for a set term, with a penalty for early withdrawal. Regular savings pay less but let you access funds anytime. Match the choice to when you'll need the money.

title: Best business loans in Nigeria (2026)
intro: Business loans in Nigeria run from quick unsecured working-capital facilities to multi-million-naira term loans, asset finance and trade finance. The right option depends on what you're funding (cash-flow gaps, equipment, expansion or imports), how much security you can offer, and your turnover history. Bank SME loans carry the lowest rates but ask for CAC registration, a business account and bank statements; finance companies and microfinance lenders are faster but pricier. We convert every product to a comparable annual basis and show fees alongside the rate, and we list only providers licensed by the Central Bank of Nigeria. Sort by interest, fees or amount, and confirm exact terms with the provider before applying — figures are indicative and change often.

faq.question: What do I need to apply for a business loan in Nigeria?
faq.answer: Most lenders require CAC registration, a business bank account, and 6–12 months of bank statements; larger facilities also ask for financial statements and a business plan. Each product lists its required documents.

faq.question: Secured or unsecured?
faq.answer: Smaller working-capital loans may be unsecured; larger term loans, asset finance and trade finance are usually secured against the asset or supported by your turnover. Secured facilities generally carry lower rates.

faq.question: Are these rates guaranteed?

title: Best credit cards in Nigeria (2026)
intro: Credit cards in Nigeria range from low-fee classic cards to premium cards with airport-lounge access, travel insurance and dollar-spend options. The figures that matter most are the purchase APR (what you pay if you carry a balance), the annual fee, and the interest-free period — pay your statement in full within it and you pay no purchase interest at all. We show the purchase APR on a comparable annual basis next to the annual fee and credit limit, and we list only cards from CBN-licensed banks. Sort by APR or fees, and confirm exact terms with the issuer — figures are indicative and change.

faq.question: How do I avoid paying interest on a credit card?
faq.answer: Pay your full statement balance within the interest-free period (often up to 45 days). You then pay no purchase interest — only the annual fee, if any. Carrying a balance is what triggers the purchase APR.

faq.question: What does the purchase APR mean?
faq.answer: It's the annual interest rate charged on balances you don't pay off in full. Our credit-card cost calculator shows how long a balance takes to clear and the total interest at a given APR and monthly payment.

faq.question: Are these rates and fees guaranteed?
faq.answer: No — they're indicative and can change, and your limit/APR depend on the issuer's assessment. Each card shows when we last verified it; confirm with the bank.

title: Best health insurance (HMO) plans in Nigeria (2026)
intro: Health insurance in Nigeria is mostly sold by HMOs and composite insurers, and plans vary widely on what matters: the annual cover limit, the hospital network, whether out-patient, dental, optical and maternity are included, and how reliably claims are paid. A cheap premium with a tiny limit or a thin network can cost you when you actually need care, so we show the premium, cover limit, any excess and the insurer's claims-paid ratio side by side. We list only insurers and HMOs licensed by NAICOM. Compare the all-in value, check the network and exclusions, and confirm the exact terms with the provider — figures are indicative and change.

faq.question: What should I look at beyond the premium?
faq.answer: The annual cover limit, the hospital network near you, what's included (out-patient, dental, optical, maternity), the excess/co-pay, and the insurer's claims-paid ratio. A low premium with a low limit or weak network is often false economy.

faq.question: What does claims-paid ratio mean?
faq.answer: The share of valid claims the insurer actually pays. Higher is better — it's a practical signal you'll be covered when you need it.

faq.question: Are these premiums guaranteed?
faq.answer: No — premiums are indicative, depend on age/plan/group, and change. Each plan shows when we last verified it; confirm with the provider.

title: Best life insurance in Nigeria (2026)
intro: Life insurance pays a lump sum to your family if you die during the cover period — term life is cheap and pure protection, while whole-life adds a savings/cash-value element at a higher premium. The figures that matter are the cover (sum assured) relative to the premium, the term, and the insurer's claims-paid record. We show premium-from, cover, claims ratio and any conditions side by side, for NAICOM-licensed insurers only. Use our insurance-needs calculator to size your cover, compare the value, and confirm exact terms with the insurer — figures are indicative and change.

faq.question: Term life or whole life?
faq.answer: Term life is cheaper and covers a set period — best for pure protection while you have dependants or debts. Whole life costs more but lasts for life and builds cash value. Match it to your goal.

faq.question: How much cover do I need?
faq.answer: A common rule is enough to replace several years of income plus clear outstanding debts. Our insurance-needs calculator gives a quick estimate.

faq.question: Are premiums guaranteed?
faq.answer: No — they depend on age, health and cover, and are indicative. Each policy shows when we last verified it; confirm with the insurer.

title: Best mutual funds in Nigeria (2026)
intro: Mutual funds let you invest in a professionally managed, diversified portfolio with a low minimum — from equity funds chasing growth to balanced and dollar funds. Returns are not guaranteed and past performance doesn't predict the future, so weigh the fund's risk level, its track record, the management fee and the minimum investment, not just the headline return. We show recent return, risk, minimum and fee side by side, for SEC-registered fund managers only. Use the investment-growth calculator to project outcomes, and confirm exact terms with the manager — figures are indicative and returns can fall as well as rise.

faq.question: Are returns guaranteed?
faq.answer: No. Mutual-fund returns vary with the market and can be negative. Treat past performance as context, not a promise, and match the fund's risk level to your horizon.

faq.question: What fees should I check?
faq.answer: The annual management fee is the main one — it compounds over time. Compare it against the fund's risk and track record.

faq.question: How were these ranked?
faq.answer: By default by customer rating, sponsored rows labelled. Re-sort as needed. Ranking is separate from the SEC-registration check.

title: Best money market funds in Nigeria (2026)
intro: Money market funds invest in short-term, low-risk instruments like treasury bills and commercial paper, aiming to preserve capital while paying more than a regular savings account — with daily or near-daily access to your cash. They're a popular place to park naira. The numbers to compare are the recent yield, the management fee and the minimum investment; risk is low but not zero. We show yield, risk, minimum and fee side by side, for SEC-registered managers only. Confirm exact terms with the manager — yields are indicative and move with interest rates.

faq.question: Is a money market fund the same as a savings account?
faq.answer: No — it's an investment, not a deposit, so it isn't a bank account and returns aren't fixed. But it's low-risk and usually pays more than savings, with easy access.

faq.question: Can I lose money?
faq.answer: Losses are rare for money market funds but not impossible; they're low-risk, not no-risk. Yields also move with interest rates.

faq.question: Are yields guaranteed?
faq.answer: No — they're indicative and change. Each fund shows when we last verified it; confirm with the manager.

title: Best pension funds (PFAs) in Nigeria (2026)
intro: Your pension is run by a Pension Fund Administrator (PFA) under the contributory scheme, and you're free to choose or switch yours. Returns differ between PFAs and between the multi-fund types (Fund I–IV, by age/risk appetite), and fees and service quality matter over decades. We show recent return, risk/fund type and the management fee side by side, for PFAs licensed by PenCom only. Use the investment-growth calculator to project your retirement pot, compare PFAs on long-run return and service, and confirm details with the PFA — figures are indicative.

faq.question: Can I change my PFA?
faq.answer: Yes — under PenCom rules you can transfer your Retirement Savings Account between PFAs (typically once a year). Long-run return and service quality are the things to compare.

faq.question: What are Fund I–IV?
faq.answer: The multi-fund structure: more aggressive funds for younger contributors, more conservative ones as you approach retirement. Your age determines the default, and you can opt within limits.

faq.question: Are returns guaranteed?
faq.answer: No — pension returns vary by PFA and fund and are indicative. Confirm with the PFA.

title: Best ways to send money within Nigeria (2026)

Some apps offer free peer-to-peer transfers; banks charge a small NIP fee. We show the transfer fee, speed and coverage side by side, for CBN-licensed providers only. Compare the real per-transfer cost for how you actually send, and confirm current fees with the provider — figures are indicative and change.

faq.question: Why are some transfers free?
faq.answer: Some fintechs subsidise peer-to-peer transfers within their own network. Bank transfers via NIP usually carry a small regulated fee. Check the fee for the destination you actually use.

faq.question: How fast are transfers?
faq.answer: Local NIP transfers are typically instant. Delays usually come from limits, downtime or compliance checks rather than the rail itself.

faq.question: Are fees guaranteed?
faq.answer: No — fees are indicative and can change. Each provider shows when we last verified it.

title: Cheapest ways to send money to Nigeria (2026)
intro: Sending money to Nigeria from abroad, the headline transfer fee is rarely the real cost — the FX margin (the gap between the rate you get and the mid-market rate) usually matters more. Diaspora-focused apps now offer low or zero fees and tighter margins on the major UK, US, Canada and Europe corridors. We show the fee, FX margin, speed and supported corridors side by side, for CBN-licensed IMTOs and payment providers only. Use our remittance-cost calculator to see what actually arrives, and confirm live rates with the provider — figures are indicative and move constantly.

faq.question: Why compare FX margin, not just the fee?
faq.answer: A 'zero-fee' transfer can still be expensive if the exchange rate is poor. The FX margin is often the bigger cost — our calculator shows the amount that actually arrives after both.

faq.question: Which corridors are covered?
faq.answer: The major diaspora corridors into Nigeria (UK, US, Canada, Europe). Each provider lists the corridors it supports.

faq.question: Are rates guaranteed?
faq.answer: No — fees and FX margins move constantly. Each provider shows when we last verified it; always confirm the live quote before sending.

title: Best payday & instant loans in Nigeria (2026)
intro: Payday loans in Nigeria are short-term advances — usually one to three months — meant to bridge the gap to your next salary. They are fast and need no collateral, but they are also the most expensive way to borrow: lenders quote a small 'monthly' interest figure that compounds into a very high annual rate once management and processing fees are added. We list only products from CBN-licensed banks and microfinance lenders, convert every offer to a comparable basis, and show the fees beside the rate so you can see the true cost. Borrow only what you can repay on time, and confirm exact terms with the lender — figures here are indicative.

faq.question: Are payday loans expensive?
faq.answer: Yes. A 'small' monthly rate can translate into a very high annual cost once fees are included. Use them only for genuine short-term needs and repay on schedule.

faq.question: Do I need collateral?
faq.answer: No — these are unsecured advances based on your salary or transaction history. You'll usually need a BVN and an active account.

title: Best asset & vehicle finance in Nigeria (2026)
intro: Asset finance lets you acquire a vehicle, generator or equipment now and spread the cost over one to five years, with the asset itself serving as security. Banks typically require an equity contribution of 20–30% and bundle insurance into the facility. The headline interest rate is only part of the cost — management fees, insurance and the size of your down payment all change what you actually pay. We compare licensed banks side by side on rate, fees, amount and tenor so you can match the repayment to your cash flow. Confirm exact terms with the lender before you commit; figures here are indicative.

faq.question: How much deposit do I need?
faq.answer: Most lenders ask for a 20–30% equity contribution, with the financed asset used as collateral for the balance.

faq.question: What can I finance?
faq.answer: New and fairly used vehicles, plant and machinery, generators and business equipment are the most common.

title: Best mortgages & home loans in Nigeria (2026)
intro: A mortgage spreads the cost of buying or building a home over as long as twenty years, with the property as security. In Nigeria you'll typically need an equity contribution of 20–30%, plus legal and valuation fees on top of the interest rate. Because the loan runs for so long, even a small rate difference changes the total cost by millions of naira, so it pays to compare carefully. We list home loans from CBN-licensed banks on rate, fees, amount and tenor, and flag which lenders are licence-checked and have claimed their listing. Always confirm the exact terms and total cost with the bank — figures here are indicative.

faq.question: How much can I borrow?
faq.answer: Usually up to 70–80% of the property value, subject to your income and the bank's affordability checks. You fund the rest as equity.

faq.question: What fees should I expect?
faq.answer: Beyond interest, budget for management, legal and valuation fees — typically a few percent of the loan — plus insurance.

title: Best trade finance in Nigeria (2026)
intro: Trade finance helps importers and exporters bridge the gap between paying suppliers and receiving goods or payment. It covers letters of credit, bills for collection, guarantees and short-term import or export loans, usually priced per quarter and backed by trade documents such as a Form M or NXP. The true cost combines the facility rate, establishment fees and any FX margin. We compare trade-finance offers from CBN-licensed banks on rate, fees, amount and tenor so businesses can find the right structure. Terms are negotiated case by case — confirm with the bank's trade desk; figures here are indicative.

faq.question: What documents do I need?
faq.answer: Typically your CAC registration, a Form M or NXP, a proforma invoice and recent bank statements. Your bank's trade desk will confirm the full list.

faq.question: Is it only for big companies?
faq.answer: No — several banks offer SME-scale trade facilities, though amounts and pricing vary with your trade history and collateral.

title: Best current accounts in Nigeria (2026)
intro: A current account is your everyday transaction account for receiving salary, paying bills and spending with a card. The traditional banks offer cheque books and wide branch networks but charge account-maintenance fees, while digital banks increasingly offer zero maintenance fees and a set number of free transfers each month. The right account depends on how you bank — branch access, transfer costs, card delivery and app quality all matter more than headline marketing. We compare current accounts on fees, minimum balance and features so you can pick the cheapest fit. Confirm current charges with the bank — figures here are indicative.

faq.question: Do current accounts pay interest?
faq.answer: Generally no — they are built for transactions, not savings. For interest, pair one with a savings account or fixed deposit.

faq.question: What fees apply?
faq.answer: The main ones are account-maintenance and transfer fees. Several digital banks now waive maintenance and offer a number of free transfers monthly.

title: Best fixed deposit rates in Nigeria (2026)
intro: A fixed deposit locks your money for a set term — typically 30 to 365 days — in exchange for a guaranteed interest rate that's higher than an ordinary savings account. The trade-off is access: withdraw early and you forfeit much of the accrued interest. Rates vary widely between banks and are often negotiable on larger balances, so comparing pays off. We list fixed-deposit products from CBN-licensed banks and microfinance banks on rate, minimum amount and tenor so you can lock in the best return for cash you won't need soon. Rates move with the market — confirm the live rate with the bank; figures here are indicative.

faq.question: Can I withdraw before maturity?
faq.answer: Usually yes, but you'll pay a pre-liquidation penalty that wipes out much of the interest earned. Only fix money you can leave untouched.

faq.question: Are the rates negotiable?
faq.answer: Often, especially on larger balances. It's worth asking the bank for a quote rather than accepting the advertised rate.

title: Best domiciliary (foreign currency) accounts in Nigeria (2026)
intro: A domiciliary account lets you hold and transact in foreign currency — usually USD, GBP or EUR — to receive remittances, pay school fees abroad, fund online purchases or save against naira depreciation. Banks differ on maintenance and withdrawal charges, how easily you can receive foreign inflows, and whether a dollar card is included. We compare domiciliary accounts from CBN-licensed banks on fees, minimum balance and features so you can find the most flexible, lowest-cost option for your foreign-currency needs. Charges and FX rules change with CBN policy — confirm current terms with the bank; figures here are indicative.

faq.question: What can I use it for?
faq.answer: Receiving foreign transfers and export proceeds, paying tuition or suppliers abroad, funding a dollar card, and holding FX savings.

faq.question: Are there withdrawal limits?
faq.answer: Cash withdrawal limits and charges vary by bank and CBN policy. Check the current rules with your bank before relying on cash access.

title: Best debit cards in Nigeria (2026)
intro: A debit card spends money you already have, linked directly to your bank account for ATM withdrawals, POS payments and online purchases. The choices come down to network acceptance (Verve for local use, Visa or Mastercard for wider reach), issuance and annual maintenance fees, and whether the card supports international or USD spending. Digital banks increasingly offer free issuance and delivery. We compare debit cards from CBN-licensed banks on fees and features so you can pick the most useful, lowest-cost card for how you actually spend. Confirm current charges with the issuer — figures here are indicative.

faq.question: Verve, Visa or Mastercard?
faq.answer: Verve is cheapest for purely local use; Visa and Mastercard add wider acceptance and some international online capability, often at a higher fee.

faq.question: Can I spend abroad?
faq.answer: Naira debit cards have limited international use. For reliable foreign spending, consider a USD card linked to a domiciliary account.

title: Best prepaid cards in Nigeria (2026)
intro: A prepaid card holds a balance you load in advance, so you can only spend what's on it — useful for budgeting, giving allowances, or paying online without exposing your main account. Most don't require a full bank account, and some come in USD for foreign online subscriptions. The things that differ are issuance and reload fees, whether the card is naira or dollar, and where it's accepted. We compare prepaid cards from CBN-licensed banks on fees and features so you can find a card that fits controlled or gift spending. Confirm current charges with the issuer — figures here are indicative.

faq.question: How is a prepaid card different from debit?
faq.answer: A debit card draws from your bank account; a prepaid card only spends the balance you've loaded onto it, which makes it good for budgeting and gifting.

faq.question: Can I use one for online subscriptions?
faq.answer: Yes — a USD prepaid card is a common way to pay for foreign streaming and software subscriptions without a domiciliary account.

title: Best virtual cards in Nigeria (2026)
intro: A virtual card is a card number you create instantly in an app, with no physical plastic — ideal for safe online payments and foreign subscriptions because you can freeze or delete it the moment you're done. Banks and fintechs offer naira and USD versions; the differences are creation and transaction fees, how the card is funded, and whether it works for international merchants. We compare virtual cards from CBN-licensed banks and fintechs on fees and features so you can pick the safest, cheapest option for online spending. Card availability and USD funding shift with CBN policy — confirm current terms with the issuer; figures here are indicative.

faq.question: Why use a virtual card?
faq.answer: Security and control: you can generate it for a single purchase or subscription and freeze or delete it instantly, keeping your main card details private.

faq.question: Do virtual dollar cards work for Netflix or AWS?
faq.answer: Often yes, but USD virtual-card funding and limits change with CBN policy. Check the issuer's current support before relying on one.

title: Best car (motor) insurance in Nigeria (2026)
intro: Motor insurance in Nigeria ranges from the statutory third-party minimum — which only covers damage and injury you cause to others — to comprehensive cover that also pays for your own vehicle against accident, fire and theft. The premium depends on the car's value, but the claims-paid ratio and the excess you bear on each claim matter just as much as the price. We compare NAICOM-licensed insurers on premium, sum insured, claims ratio and excess so you can judge cover, not just cost. Read the policy exclusions and confirm terms with the insurer — figures here are indicative.

faq.question: Third-party or comprehensive?
faq.answer: Third-party is the cheap legal minimum and only covers others. Comprehensive also covers your own car for accident, fire and theft — worth it for newer or financed vehicles.

faq.question: Why does the claims ratio matter?
faq.answer: It signals how reliably an insurer actually pays. A low premium is poor value if claims are routinely delayed or declined.

title: Best travel insurance in Nigeria (2026)
intro: Travel insurance covers medical emergencies, evacuation, trip cancellation and lost baggage while you're abroad — and a Schengen- or visa-compliant policy is mandatory for many visa applications. Cover levels, the medical sum insured and what counts as an excludable pre-existing condition vary a lot between insurers, so the cheapest policy isn't always the one that pays when it matters. We compare NAICOM-licensed insurers on premium, sum insured and claims record so you can match the cover to your trip and visa requirements. Always read the policy wording and confirm with the insurer — figures here are indicative.

faq.question: Do I need it for a visa?
faq.answer: Yes for many — Schengen and several other visas require travel insurance with a minimum medical cover, usually around €30,000. Check your destination's rule.

faq.question: What does it actually cover?
faq.answer: Typically emergency medical treatment and evacuation, trip cancellation or delay, and lost or delayed baggage. Pre-existing conditions are often excluded unless declared.

title: Best business & SME insurance in Nigeria (2026)
intro: Business insurance protects your premises, stock, equipment and people against fire, burglary, liability claims and business interruption — and some cover, such as group life for employees, is a legal requirement. Policies are usually bundled, so the right one depends on your assets and risks rather than headline price alone; the claims-paid ratio and the excess you carry are key. We compare NAICOM-licensed insurers on premium, sum insured, claims ratio and excess so SMEs can protect the business without overpaying. Have your assets professionally valued and confirm the policy scope with the insurer — figures here are indicative.

faq.question: Is any business cover compulsory?
faq.answer: Group life cover for employees is statutory for registered employers, and some sectors require specific liability cover. Check the rules for your industry.

faq.question: What should an SME prioritise?
faq.answer: Usually fire and special perils on premises and stock, public liability, and — if you have staff — group life. Bundle policies often cost less than buying each separately.

title: Best agricultural insurance in Nigeria (2026)
intro: Agricultural insurance protects farmers against the losses that weather, pests, disease and other named perils inflict on crops and livestock. Policies range from named-peril and multi-peril crop cover to livestock and poultry mortality cover, and increasingly index-based products that pay out on measured rainfall rather than individual loss assessment. Premiums are modest relative to the sum insured, but payout terms and excesses differ, so the structure matters. We compare NAICOM-licensed insurers on premium, sum insured, claims ratio and excess so farmers and cooperatives can protect their season. Confirm the cover and exclusions with the insurer — figures here are indicative.

faq.question: What perils are covered?
faq.answer: Commonly drought, flood, storm, fire, pests and disease for crops, and death or disease for livestock and poultry. Index-based policies pay on measured weather data.

faq.question: Can cooperatives get cover?
faq.answer: Yes — several insurers price cover for farmer cooperatives and smallholder groups, which can be cheaper than buying individually.

title: Best fixed-income & bond funds in Nigeria (2026)
intro: Fixed-income funds invest in government and corporate bonds and treasury bills to deliver steadier, more predictable returns than equity funds, with lower risk. Naira funds track local yields, while eurobond funds give USD-denominated returns for investors hedging against naira depreciation. The headline yield matters, but so do the management fee, the minimum investment and how the fund balances income against capital stability. We compare SEC-registered fund managers on return, risk, minimum investment and fee so you can park cash for income without taking equity risk. Returns are not guaranteed and move with rates — confirm with the manager; figures here are indicative.

faq.question: How is this different from a money-market fund?
faq.answer: Money-market funds hold very short-term instruments and aim purely for stability; fixed-income funds add longer bonds for higher yield, with slightly more price movement.

faq.question: Naira or dollar fund?
faq.answer: Naira funds offer higher headline yields; eurobond (USD) funds offer lower yields but hedge against naira depreciation. Many investors hold both.

title: Best FX & currency exchange services in Nigeria (2026)
intro: Foreign-exchange services cover converting and sending currency for school fees, supplier payments, PTA/BTA travel allowances and business settlement. Banks handle SWIFT wires and trade FX from a domiciliary account, while fintechs offer multicurrency wallets with tighter margins on the major corridors. The real cost is the transfer fee plus the FX margin — the gap between your rate and the mid-market rate — which usually dwarfs the visible fee. We compare CBN-licensed banks and payment providers on fee, FX margin, speed and supported currencies so you keep more of your money. Rates move constantly with CBN policy — confirm the live quote; figures here are indicative.

faq.question: Why is the FX margin so important?
faq.answer: A low or zero transfer fee can hide a poor exchange rate. The FX margin is often the bigger cost, so always compare the rate you actually receive.

faq.question: Bank or fintech for FX?
faq.answer: Banks suit large, document-backed trade and SWIFT transfers; fintech multicurrency wallets often give tighter margins and faster delivery on everyday amounts.
